newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Prince Charles bestows last honours on HK Chinese.
newsitem.headline: Prince Charles bestows last honours on HK Chinese.

text.p: Prince Charles performed a dying rite of empire on Sunday, handing out British honours in the gilded ballroom of Hong Kong's Government House that may soon become a museum.

As a police band played the Beatles classic "Yesterday," the British royal heir gave out the last awards granted to local Chinese dignitaries before he officiates at Monday's midnight ceremony to hand Hong Kong back to China.
The decorations, rewarding loyalty to colonial rule, are being replaced by Hong Kong's own insignia for its new era as an autonomous Special Administrative Region in China.
Billionaire industrialist Gordon Wu and Financial Secretary Donald Tsang knelt on a stool brought especially out from Buckingham Palace as they were knighted by Queen Elizabeth's son.
Wu, knighted for services to British exports, still plans to use the honour once communist China takes over this thriving capitalist enclave.
"The prince asked me whether I would still wear it (the insignia) and I said "Of course, I have earned it,'" Wu said after the elegant ceremony held beneath glittering chandeliers.
Tsang, sporting his trademark bow tie for the grandiose ceremony, was more circumspect about his honour.
"I think it is very sweet, I wouldn't say it is irrelevant. I treasure it. My affiliation is to the Hong Kong people and this is why I got it. But this now of course becomes a foreign decoration."

An aide de camp intoned the name of each recipient. Charles, in crisp white naval uniform, offered 116 smiles and handshakes of congratulation to everyone from a headmistress to a doctor of Chinese traditional medicine.

The band made its own tuneful commentary on the centuries-old ceremony, playing "Strangers in Paradise" before moving onto "I Did It My Way"-- apparent echoes of traditional colonial swagger in an outpost seized from China 156 years ago.

One of the biggest rounds of applause greeted helicopter winchman Jason Chan Siu-kei who won the Queen's gallantry medal. He rescued five children from a hill fire despite receiving burns to his face and neck.
Posing proudly for his family afterwards on the lawn of Government House, the governor's residence, he said: "At the time I did think about my life, whether I could survive or not.
"It was a very dangerous moment on a cliff with very frightened children. But you have to stay calm."
Hong Kong's new rulers have set up their own system of honours, awarding the Grand Bauhinia Medal which is named after the blossom that will be the emblem of Hong Kong.
Gordon Wu had no hesitation about the choice he would make if offered one of these medals. "I would take it."
The last Governor, Chris Patten, leaves aboard the royal yacht Britannia with Prince Charles early on Tuesday after the midnight ceremony.
The fate of Government House in the heart of Hong Kong is uncertain. It may be used for state functions or as a museum.

His replacement, China's anointed chief executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa, has chosen to stay on in his own hillside apartment - in an exclusive area where the British once refused to allow Chinese to establish homes.
